terms.definition: The noon-day demon. The spiritual torpor that afflicts monks at midday — not laziness but the inability to care: a profound indifference to one's own salvation and to the world. Cassian and Evagrius Ponticus described it as the most dangerous of the eight passions because it mimics rest while being its opposite. Aquinas made it a capital sin. Cioran, Baudelaire, and the entire tradition of ennui are secular descendants. Agamben: acedia is the refusal to will one's own possibility.
terms.etymology: Latin from Greek akēdia: a- (without) + kēdos (care, grief). The medieval 'sloth' translation impoverishes the concept.

terms.definition: Refined conduct, literary culture, the ethics of comportment. In classical Arabic usage: the body of knowledge and behaviour expected of a cultivated person — proper manners, command of poetry, historical learning, controlled emotion. In Persian court culture: the entire civilisational complex of letters, etiquette, and aesthetic refinement. The adīb (man of adab) is the Islamic humanist. The concept has no single Western equivalent: it is simultaneously Bildung, courtesy, and literary canon.
terms.etymology: Arabic root أ-د-ب (ʾ-d-b): to discipline, to invite to a banquet. The sense expanded from table manners to all of culture.

terms.definition: Abu Dhabi's financial free zone — established 2015, operates under common law. Regulator is FSRA (Financial Services Regulatory Authority). Competes with DIFC for regional financial services. Located on Al Maryah Island.
terms.etymology: Abu Dhabi Global Market.

terms.definition: German stock corporation — the form for publicly traded companies. Requires minimum €50,000 share capital. Governed by AktG (Aktiengesetz). Has a two-tier board structure: Vorstand (management board) and Aufsichtsrat (supervisory board). Used throughout German-speaking countries.
terms.etymology: Aktien (shares, stocks) + Gesellschaft (company, society).

terms.definition: Acting out — repeating in action what cannot be remembered. Freud's concept: the patient who cannot recall a repressed memory will instead repeat it, compulsively enacting it in the present rather than making it conscious. The neurotic does not remember the primal scene; they re-live it in every relationship. Psychoanalytic treatment is the conversion of repetition into remembering. Politically: nations that cannot mourn their past act it out — Freud's own argument about post-WWI Germany.
terms.etymology: From Latin agere (to do, to act). Freud's German term; the English 'acting out' is the standard translation.

terms.definition: Struggle, contest — the principle of organised conflict that the Greeks considered essential to excellence. The Olympic Games, the tragic festival, the law court, the philosophical dialogue: all are agōnes. Nietzsche's Homer's Contest argues that Greek culture was built on the agonistic impulse — the excellence-generating rivalry that required worthy opponents. Without the agōn, culture does not simply become peaceful; it becomes mediocre.
terms.etymology: Greek: contest, struggle. Root of agony, protagonist, antagonist.

terms.definition: Non-harming. The ethical principle central to Jainism, Buddhism, and Hinduism: the refusal to cause harm to any living being. In Jainism, the absolute principle. In Gandhi's political programme, transformed into a technique of resistance: ahiṃsā not as passivity but as the most demanding form of action — requiring more courage than violence because it refuses the easy exit of retaliation.
terms.etymology: A- (non-) + hiṃsā (harm, violence), from the root han (to strike). First appears in the Chandogya Upanishad.

terms.definition: Truth as unconcealment. Not correctness (a statement matching a fact) but disclosure — the showing-forth of what was hidden. Heidegger's reading: truth is not a property of propositions but an event of unconcealment. The river shows what was always there. The etymology matters: a-letheia, the un-forgotten.
terms.etymology: A- (un-) + lethe (forgetting, concealment). Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Hades.

terms.definition: Love of fate; the attitude of not merely accepting but embracing everything that happens, including suffering and loss.
terms.etymology: Amor (love) + fati (of fate)
terms.usage: Nietzsche advocated amor fati as the highest formula of affirmation.

terms.definition: The analogy of being. The Catholic metaphysical claim that creation participates in God's being without being identical to it — beings are neither wholly different from God (equivocal) nor the same (univocal) but analogous. The analogia entis makes natural theology possible: we can reason from the world toward God because they share a proportional relationship. Karl Barth called it 'the invention of the Antichrist' — the attempt to reach God by human reason rather than revelation. The debate between Barth and Przywara defines 20th-century theology.
terms.etymology: Analogia (Greek analogia: proportion) + entis (Latin genitive of ens, being). Systematised by Thomas Aquinas.

terms.definition: The old order; the political and social system of France before the Revolution of 1789, characterized by monarchy, aristocratic privilege, and feudal vestiges.
terms.etymology: Ancien (old, former) + régime (system, order)
terms.usage: Tocqueville analyzed how the ancien régime's centralization persisted through revolution.

terms.definition: Normlessness. Durkheim's concept: the condition when social norms have broken down and individuals lose their sense of moral orientation. Not simply lawlessness but the absence of shared standards for evaluating behaviour. Durkheim found it in suicide statistics — rising anomie correlates with rising self-destruction. It is the pathology of freedom without structure.
terms.etymology: From Greek a- (without) + nomos (law, norm). Durkheim introduced the sociological sense in Le Suicide (1897).

terms.definition: The spontaneous perception of connections and meaningfulness in unrelated things. Klaus Conrad coined it (1958) as a clinical term for early psychosis: the patient begins to find hidden significance everywhere — in licence plates, overheard conversations, the arrangement of objects. Extended by Philip K. Dick and conspiracy theory researchers: the pathology that underlies pattern-recognition, the capacity that makes both science and paranoia possible. The same cognitive machinery finds the signal and the noise.
terms.etymology: Greek apo (away from) + phaenein (to show). Conrad distinguished it from anaesthesia (the loss of meaning) — apophenia is its excess.

terms.definition: Impasse, perplexity. The state of not knowing — the productive confusion at the end of a Socratic dialogue when all positions have been shown to be untenable and the interlocutor admits they do not know what they thought they knew. Plato's early dialogues end in aporia. It is not failure but clearing: the space where genuine inquiry begins.
terms.etymology: A- (without) + poros (passage, path). The aporia is the place where the road runs out.

terms.definition: The here and now of an artwork — its unique existence at the place where it happens to be, the history inscribed in its material presence. Benjamin's concept in The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction: technical reproduction destroys the aura by detaching the reproduced object from the domain of tradition. The painting in a museum has aura; its postcard does not. The concept is simultaneously a loss (of ritual, of uniqueness) and a liberation (the politicisation of art freed from its cultic function).
terms.etymology: Greek and Latin: breath, breeze, the barely perceptible emanation from an object.

quotes.text: Was im Zeitalter der technischen Reproduzierbarkeit verkümmert, ist die Aura des Kunstwerks.
quotes.source: Walter Benjamin, Das Kunstwerk im Zeitalter seiner technischen Reproduzierbarkeit, 1935

terms.definition: State of exception. Carl Schmitt's concept in Political Theology (1922): "Sovereign is he who decides on the exception." The sovereign is defined not by normal governance but by the power to suspend the legal order in emergency — and thereby reveal that the legal order depends on a pre-legal decision. Agamben extended it: the state of exception has become the permanent paradigm of government in modernity. Guantánamo, emergency powers, indefinite detention — the exception has become the rule.
terms.etymology: Ausnahme (exception) + Zustand (state, condition). Political Theology: Vier Kapitel zur Lehre von der Souveränität, 1922.

quotes.text: Souverän ist, wer über den Ausnahmezustand entscheidet.
quotes.source: Carl Schmitt, Politische Theologie, 1922

terms.definition: Beautiful but unfaithful. The French 17th–18th century tradition of translation that adapted source texts to French taste — elegant, fluent, idiomatic — at the cost of the original's foreignness. Opposed to the German Romantic tradition (Schleiermacher, Hölderlin) that sought to let the foreign remain foreign, to bring the reader to the text rather than the text to the reader. The tension between domestication (belles infidèles) and foreignisation defines all translation ethics.
terms.etymology: The phrase attributed to Gilles Ménage (17th c.) of Nicolas Perrot d'Ablancourt's translations of ancient authors.

terms.definition: Self-cultivation and formation; the process of developing one's intellectual, aesthetic, and moral capacities into a harmonious whole.
terms.etymology: From 'Bild' (image, form) - forming oneself
terms.usage: German Idealism made Bildung central to human flourishing.

terms.definition: Upheaval, overturning. A word that does more than 'revolution' — it carries the physical sensation of being turned upside down. The bouleversement is not only political but affective: a complete disorientation of the known order. French history is structured by them; the word has the weight of recurrence.
terms.etymology: From bouleverser — to overturn, from boule (ball) + verser (to pour, to turn).

terms.definition: Making do with what is at hand. Lévi-Strauss's concept in The Savage Mind: the bricoleur solves problems using whatever materials are available, unlike the engineer who acquires the right tool for the job. Mythological thought is bricolage — assembling meaning from inherited fragments. Punk is bricolage. All translation is bricolage.
terms.etymology: From bricoler — to tinker, to do odd jobs. The bricoleur is the odd-job man of thought.

terms.definition: The everyday — the material texture of ordinary life. The Russian avant-garde's great enemy and great project: the Constructivists, Productivists, and LEF group wanted to transform byt — to revolutionise not just politics but the chairs, the teapots, the daily rituals of existence. The revolution would be incomplete until the logic of the old world was removed from the domestic sphere. Byt absorbed the revolution; the revolution failed to transform byt. The concept later became central to the Situationist International's concept of "everyday life."
terms.etymology: Russian: way of life, daily routine, the everyday. From byt' (to be).

terms.definition: Seize the day; enjoy the present moment rather than placing hope in the future.
terms.etymology: Carpe (pluck, seize) + diem (day)
terms.usage: Horace's carpe diem acknowledges mortality while affirming life's pleasures.

terms.definition: An act or event that provokes or justifies war; the occasion for war.
terms.etymology: Casus (fall, occasion) + belli (of war)
terms.usage: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand provided the casus belli for World War I.

terms.definition: Positive affirmation vs negative denial as modes of theological discourse. Cataphatic: God is good, powerful, wise — positive predicates. Apophatic: God is not this, not that — via negativa. The tension between them is irreducible: the cataphatic risks anthropomorphism; the apophatic risks silence. The greatest medieval mystics — Eckhart, Dionysius, Nicholas of Cusa — tried to hold both simultaneously: 'the super-essential darkness' (Dionysius) — a language that names God by exceeding what names can do.
terms.etymology: Kataphasis: kata (according to) + phasis (statement). Apophasis: apo (away from) + phasis.

terms.definition: Unique identifier for EU legal documents — regulations, directives, decisions, case law. Format: sector + year + document type + number. Example: 32016R0679 is the GDPR. Used in EUR-Lex database. Essential for precise citation of EU law.
terms.etymology: Communitatis Europeae Lex — Latin for 'Law of the European Community'.

terms.definition: The field — Bourdieu's concept of the structured space of social positions within a domain (the literary field, the academic field, the political field). Each field has its own capital, its own rules, its own logic of competition. To enter a field is to accept its doxa — the unquestioned beliefs that structure the game. The literary field's capital is symbolic recognition; the economic field's is money. The concepts of field and habitus together explain why individuals reproduce social structures without being commanded to.
terms.etymology: French: field, domain. Physics metaphor: a force field that exerts pressures on all who enter it.

terms.definition: The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting; by extension, the interplay of contrasting elements in any art form or situation.
terms.etymology: Chiaro (clear, light) + scuro (dark, obscure)
terms.usage: Caravaggio mastered chiaroscuro to create dramatic psychological intensity.

terms.definition: Destruction, catastrophe. Originally the destruction of the First Temple (586 BCE) and Second Temple (70 CE). Extended to the Holocaust — many Eastern European Jews initially called it the Churban rather than Shoah. The word carries the theology of destruction as rupture in the covenant, followed by mourning, and the possibility of return. A word that names not just destruction but its specific structure: the destruction of what was sacred.
terms.etymology: From the root ח-ר-ב (ḥ-r-b), meaning desolation, ruin. The same root as ḥorev (sword).

terms.definition: I think, therefore I am; Descartes' foundational certainty that the very act of doubting proves the existence of the thinking self.
terms.etymology: Cogito (I think) + ergo (therefore) + sum (I am)
terms.usage: The cogito established the basis for modern rationalist philosophy.

terms.definition: The inner voice. Not a demon (the Christian word is a corruption of this) but an intermediary spirit — the voice that tells Socrates not to do certain things, never what to do. The daimon is the individual's attendant spirit, sometimes genius, sometimes divine warning. Heidegger paraphrased Heraclitus: ēthos anthrōpōi daimōn — character is fate.
terms.etymology: Perhaps from daiomai (to divide, to distribute) — the daimon distributes one's portion.

terms.definition: Condemnation of memory. The Roman practice of erasing a person from the historical record — removing inscriptions, melting statues, burning documents — as if they had never existed. A punishment beyond death. Soviet airbrushing, Twitter deplatforming, colonial statue-removal: all are damnatio memoriae, though only the Roman original was legally codified.
terms.etymology: Damnatio (condemnation, from damnare) + memoriae (genitive of memoria, memory).

terms.definition: The Thing — the unrepresentable real object that desire circles without reaching. Freud's concept in Project for a Scientific Psychology, systematised by Lacan in Seminar VII: the Ethics of Psychoanalysis. Das Ding is not an object in the world but the void around which the world of objects is organised — the original lost object (the mother's body) whose loss constitutes desire. Art is the construction of a Thing — a beautiful object that surrounds the void without filling it.
terms.etymology: German: the thing. Distinguished from das Objekt (the object of desire, which is always a substitute).

terms.definition: Being-there; Heidegger's term for human existence characterized by its unique awareness of and concern for its own being.
terms.etymology: Da (there) + Sein (being)
terms.usage: Dasein's fundamental structure is being-in-the-world.

terms.definition: The heart as the organ of intuitive knowledge. Not the seat of sentiment — the Persian del is where perception, wisdom, and mystical illumination converge. The Sufi tradition distinguishes between the 'aql (discursive reason, which circles) and the del (the heart, which sees directly). Rumi's entire poetics is addressed to the del: the reed flute cries because the del has been separated from its origin.
terms.etymology: From Middle Persian dil. Cognate with Latin cor, Greek kardia — but the Persian concept is closer to nous than to 'heart.'

terms.definition: The art of getting out of a tight spot through improvisation and creative resourcefulness. The specifically Portuguese capacity to solve problems with insufficient means and no plan — not mere muddling through but an almost aesthetic commitment to last-minute improvisation. Related to the Brazilian jeitinho but less focused on social manipulation, more on practical ingenuity.
terms.etymology: From desenrascar — to un-trap, to disentangle (des- + enrascar, to get caught in a trap). The suffix -anço makes it an art or practice.

terms.definition: The blood levy. The Ottoman practice of conscripting Christian boys — primarily from the Balkans — converting them to Islam and training them for elite military and administrative service as janissaries and palace officials. The system produced the empire's most loyal servants precisely because they had no other allegiance: no tribe, no family inheritance, no competing loyalty. Paradox: the empire's strength came from those it had uprooted. Many of its greatest grand viziers were devşirme boys.
terms.etymology: From devşirmek (to collect, to levy). The system operated c. 1380–1648.

terms.definition: Decisionism — the doctrine that the ultimate ground of political order is not reason, norm, or value but a pure decision. Schmitt's position: the legal order is not self-grounding; it rests on a primordial act of will that cannot be derived from anything else. The decision precedes the norm. This is both a political critique (liberalism's pretence of normative self-sufficiency) and a vulnerability (it makes power the ultimate reality). Weber's polytheism of values and Nietzsche's will to power are its philosophical relatives.
terms.etymology: From Latin decisio (decision, cutting through). Schmitt's term for the primacy of the will over the norm.

terms.definition: The statute governing corporations incorporated in Delaware — the most influential corporate law in America. More than 60% of Fortune 500 companies are Delaware corporations. Known for flexibility, predictable case law from the Court of Chancery, and business-friendly provisions.
terms.etymology: Delaware + General Corporation Law.

terms.definition: The principle that holds things in their proper place. Not 'duty' — that translation collapses a cosmic concept into a social one. Dharma is what keeps the universe from dissolving into chaos: the order that is simultaneously natural law, social norm, ethical obligation, and religious practice. Each being has its own dharma (svadharma) — the right action appropriate to its nature and station. The Bhagavad Gita's central problem: Arjuna must follow his dharma as a warrior even when it produces suffering.
terms.etymology: Sanskrit root dhṛ (to hold, to support). Cognate with Latin firmus. Appears in the Rigveda.

terms.definition: Dialectical image. Benjamin's concept in the Arcades Project: the image where the Then (das Gewesene) and the Now (das Jetzt) flash together in a constellation. Not a temporal sequence (this caused that) but a spatial figure — a now charged with a particular past that only this present can read. The dialectical image is what historical knowledge looks like when it is political: the moment when the oppressed recognise their situation in the past and the past speaks to the present.
terms.etymology: Dialectical (Hegelian) + Bild (image, picture). Benjamin's term for the non-narrative structure of historical understanding.

quotes.text: Bild ist dasjenige, worin das Gewesene mit dem Jetzt blitzhaft zu einer Konstellation zusammentritt.
quotes.source: Walter Benjamin, Arcades Project, N2a,3

terms.definition: Dubai's financial free zone — operates under common law (based on English law), separate from UAE civil law. Has its own courts (DIFC Courts) and regulator (DFSA). Popular for regional headquarters, funds, and financial services. Companies can be 100% foreign-owned.
terms.etymology: Dubai International Financial Centre.

terms.definition: Derrida's neologism — neither différence (difference) nor différance as an existing word, but a coinage that is visually distinct and aurally identical to différence in French. It cannot be heard, only read. The concept names the double movement by which meaning is produced: signs differ from one another (spatial difference) and defer their meaning indefinitely (temporal deferral). There is no moment when the sign reaches its referent, no presence behind the signifier. The unpronounceable word performs its own argument.
terms.etymology: Derrida's portmanteau: différer (to differ) + différer (to defer) + the -ance suffix. Introduced in a 1968 lecture.

quotes.text: La différance n'est pas, n'existe pas, n'est pas un étant-présent.
quotes.source: Jacques Derrida, La Différance, 1968

terms.definition: The apparatus — a network of discourses, institutions, architectures, laws, and practices that together capture, orient, and govern living beings. Foucault's concept, systematised by Agamben: the dispositif is not merely a tool but an assemblage that produces subjects. The prison, the school, the hospital, the confessional are all dispositifs. Agamben: any dispositif implies a process of subjectification — it makes a subject out of a living being, and the subject is always already captured.
terms.etymology: French: device, mechanism, apparatus. Foucault introduced it in an interview in 1977.

terms.definition: The sweetness of doing nothing; pleasant idleness elevated to an art form.
terms.etymology: Dolce (sweet) + far (to do) + niente (nothing)
terms.usage: The Italian concept of dolce far niente stands in contrast to Protestant work ethics.

terms.definition: Received opinion — the unquestioned beliefs that structure a field or a society. In Plato, doxa is mere opinion, opposed to episteme (true knowledge). In Bourdieu, the doxa of a field is what goes without saying — the presuppositions so basic they are never questioned. The political operation of doxa: making contingent arrangements appear natural. The critical task: converting doxa into opinion (recognisable as a position) — which is already half of ideology critique.
terms.etymology: Greek: opinion, glory, seeming. From dokein (to seem, to think). Bourdieu recovered it for sociology.

terms.definition: The dark spirit of art. Lorca's concept: the mysterious force that animates great flamenco, bull-fighting, and poetry — not inspiration, not charm, but a kind of wound, a nearness to death. The duende cannot be summoned by technique alone; it comes only when the artist is at the edge. 'All that has dark sounds has duende.' It is the aesthetic force that confronts the problem of death rather than decorating it.
terms.etymology: From Spanish folk tradition: a goblin or spirit who inhabits a house. Lorca theorised it in Juego y teoría del duende (1933).

terms.definition: While I breathe, I hope. Cicero's formula — the minimum philosophical position, the basis below which no further reduction is possible. Not optimism (which requires evidence) but something prior: the bare orientation toward the future that is inseparable from continued existence. Agamben: it is also the formula of biopolitics — the reduction of political life to bare life, mere breathing, survives as the last claim to significance.
terms.etymology: Dum (while) + spiro (I breathe, from spirare) + spero (I hope, from sperare). The alliteration is the argument: breath and hope share a root.

terms.definition: Standardized citation system for European court decisions. Format: ECLI:country:court:year:number. Example: ECLI:EU:C:2014:2454 (Google Spain). Enables uniform citation across jurisdictions. Adopted by CJEU, ECHR, and many national courts.
terms.etymology: European Case Law Identifier.

terms.definition: Hegemony — consent manufactured into domination. Gramsci's Prison Notebooks concept: the ruling class does not maintain power through force alone but through cultural leadership — making its worldview appear as common sense, natural, inevitable. Hegemony is the achievement of consent from the dominated. Counter-hegemony requires a "war of position" — the slow construction of alternative institutions, values, and intellectual leadership before any seizure of power. The concept transformed how the left thought about culture and ideology.
terms.etymology: From Greek hēgemonia (leadership, dominance). Gramsci distinguished it from domination (direct coercion).

quotes.text: The State is the entire complex of practical and theoretical activities with which the ruling class not only justifies and maintains its dominance, but manages to win the active consent of those over whom it rules.
quotes.source: Antonio Gramsci, Prison Notebooks

terms.definition: The verbal description of a visual work — language competing with image. Homer's description of Achilles' shield is the paradigm: the poem makes you see what cannot be seen, generates a world from words alone. The technique is both ancient exercise and modernist obsession: Keats's Ode on a Grecian Urn, Auden's Musée des Beaux Arts. Ekphrasis raises the question that haunts all representation: can language capture what only image can show, can image capture what only language can say?
terms.etymology: Greek: ek (out) + phrazein (to speak, to express). A complete, vivid description.

quotes.text: On it he made the earth and sky and sea, the weariless sun, the moon at the full, and all the signs that crown the heavens.
quotes.source: Homer, Iliad, XVIII (on the Shield of Achilles)

terms.definition: The point in space that contains all other points. Borges's 1945 story: in the basement of a house on Garay Street, Buenos Aires, the narrator sees the Aleph — a small iridescent sphere of about two or three centimetres, in which the entire universe is visible simultaneously, from every angle, without confusion. Not a metaphor. The Aleph is the paradox of the infinite contained in the finite — the library that contains all books, the map at 1:1 scale. The name of this project.
terms.etymology: First letter of the Hebrew alphabet — א — also the first infinite cardinal number in Cantor's set theory (ℵ₀). The point where language, mathematics, and mysticism converge.

terms.definition: Vivid bringing-before-the-eyes — making the absent present through speech. The rhetorical ideal of vividness: the description so precise that the listener sees the scene as if present. Quintilian: evidentia, the quality of making absent things apparent. Distinct from simple clarity: enargeia is the force that makes language cross the threshold from statement to experience. Benjamin's dialectical image and Barthes's punctum are its modern descendants.
terms.etymology: Greek: en (in) + argos (shining, bright). The word that is also at the root of "energy."

terms.definition: A feeling of listlessness and dissatisfaction arising from lack of occupation or interest; existential boredom that goes beyond mere tedium.
terms.etymology: From Old French 'enui' (annoyance), from Latin 'in odio' (in hatred)
terms.usage: Baudelaire made ennui the central malaise of modern existence in Les Fleurs du mal.

terms.definition: Alienation; the estrangement of individuals from their labor, fellow humans, or essential nature. Key concept in Marxist and existentialist thought.
terms.etymology: From 'entfremden' (to alienate), from 'fremd' (foreign, strange)
terms.usage: Marx argued that capitalism produces Entfremdung by separating workers from the products of their labor.

terms.definition: Out of nothing. The theological claim that God created the world from nothing — not from pre-existing matter. The philosophical problem: nothing cannot be the cause of something. Artistic creation ex nihilo is the Romantic fantasy of the artist as god; all actual creation is bricolage.
terms.etymology: Ex (out of) + nihilo (ablative of nihil, nothing). 'Nihilism' derives from nihil.

terms.definition: Half-timbered house. The building type where the structural skeleton is exposed — timber frame visible, spaces filled with wattle or plaster. A technology of honesty: the structure is the ornament. Ruskin would have approved. The aesthetic that refuses to hide how a thing is made.
terms.etymology: Fachwerk (framework, from Fach — panel + Werk — work) + Haus (house).

terms.definition: One who lives by and through fado. Not simply a singer but a person whose character is shaped by the music's melancholic fatalism — the sense that one's fate (fado) is inescapable and beautiful. The Alfama fadistas of Lisbon carried a specific social type: poverty, dignity, defiant grief.
terms.etymology: From fado (fate, destiny) + -ista. Fado derives from Latin fatum.

terms.definition: Annihilation of the self in God. The Sufi station of ego-dissolution — the final stage of the mystical path, where the individual self is extinguished in the divine. Al-Hallaj: ana'l-Haqq (I am the Truth) — the utterance that got him executed, because it could be heard as blasphemy or as the logical endpoint of fanāʾ: the self so dissolved that only God remains to speak. Distinguishable from mere death by the companion concept baqāʾ (subsistence) — after annihilation, a purified existence continues.
terms.etymology: Arabic root ف-ن-ي (f-n-y): to perish, to pass away. Introduced as a technical term by Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri (9th c.) and systematised by al-Junayd.

terms.definition: Divine glory, the luminous kingship aura. In Zoroastrian cosmology, the farr is the sign of legitimate sovereignty — visible radiance that attaches to righteous rulers and abandons tyrants the moment they transgress. When Jamshid became proud, the farr fled him in the form of a bird. It is not merely charisma but a cosmic verdict: the universe withdrawing its endorsement.
terms.etymology: Avestan xvarənah. The concept runs from the Avesta through the Shahnameh into Safavid and Mughal imperial ideology.

terms.definition: Far-pain. The longing for distant places — the opposite of Heimweh (homesickness). Where Heimweh aches for what you have left, Fernweh aches for places you have never been. The traveller's disease. The world is always more interesting elsewhere.
terms.etymology: Fern (far, distant) + Weh (pain, ache). Structurally parallel to Heimweh.

terms.definition: Commodity fetishism. Marx's concept in Capital, Chapter 1: the commodity appears to have a value that belongs to it, as if it were a natural property, when in fact value is crystallised human labour — social relations between people taking on the form of relations between things. The table stands on its head and dances. The fetish attributes to an object powers that belong to human activity. The concept is both an analysis of capitalism and a theory of ideology: the systemic illusion that cannot be dissolved by mere demystification because it is produced materially.
terms.etymology: Fetish from Portuguese feitiço (charm, enchantment). Marx borrowed the anthropological concept to describe capitalism's own magic.

quotes.text: A commodity appears at first sight an extremely obvious, trivial thing. But its analysis brings out that it is a very strange thing, abounding in metaphysical subtleties and theological niceties.
quotes.source: Karl Marx, Capital, Volume I, Chapter 1, 1867

terms.definition: Let justice be done though the heavens fall. The principle that makes law something other than politics: the claim that justice must be done regardless of consequences, that the calculation of outcomes cannot override the obligation to act rightly. Both the formula and its critique have been active ever since: Kant endorsed it; Mill opposed it. The phrase identifies the fault line between deontological and consequentialist ethics, and between the rule of law and reason of state.
terms.etymology: Fiat (let it be done) + iustitia (justice) + ruat (let it fall) + caelum (heaven). Attributed to Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor; popularised by Kant.

terms.definition: Let there be light. Genesis 1:3 in the Vulgate. The performative utterance that creates by naming — language as causation, not description. Austin's speech act theory is its secular elaboration. Universities adopted it as motto (Columbia, UC system) because scholarship claimed the same creative-illuminating power.
terms.etymology: Fiat (third person singular present subjunctive of fieri: let it be, let there be) + lux (light).

terms.definition: Civil strife, temptation, chaos. The most feared concept in Islamic political thought: the internal conflict that destroys the community. The early Muslim civil wars were fitna; so was the seduction to apostasy. The word unifies political disorder and spiritual temptation — both are forms of the same dissolution. Against fitna, even an unjust ruler was preferable to chaos.
terms.etymology: From fatana (to try, to tempt, to afflict). The root covers trial, sedition, and enchantment.

terms.definition: Gone/Here. Freud's observation in Beyond the Pleasure Principle: his 18-month-old grandson threw a spool out of his cot (fort — gone) and pulled it back (da — here), repeatedly. Freud read it as the child's mastery of the mother's absence — turning passive suffering into active play, instituting representation. The origin of language, of the symbol, of culture: the capacity to make present what is absent. Lacan: the fort/da is the entry into the symbolic order — the subject is constituted in the moment they can say 'gone.'
terms.etymology: German fort (away, gone) and da (there, here). The episode is in Jenseits des Lustprinzips (1920).

terms.definition: Progress — as critique. Benjamin's angel of history (after Klee's Angelus Novus): the angel faces the past, sees the wreckage piling up, and is blown backward into the future by the storm of progress. The storm is what we call progress. The concept inverts the Enlightenment narrative: progress is not accumulation but catastrophe seen from the perspective of the defeated. The idea of progress depends on the idea that time moves forward and that forward is better — both of which Benjamin contests.
terms.etymology: Fort (forward, away) + Schritt (step). The most ordinary German word for progress; Benjamin makes it monstrous.

quotes.text: Der Engel der Geschichte... sieht eine einzige Katastrophe, die unablässig Trümmer auf Trümmer häuft.
quotes.source: Walter Benjamin, Theses on the Philosophy of History, IX, 1940

terms.definition: Open-air living; a philosophy of spending time outdoors to nurture the soul. Not just outdoor recreation but a way of life connected to nature.
terms.etymology: From fri (free) + luft (air) + liv (life)

terms.definition: Making superficial changes to preserve the existing power structure; 'everything must change so that everything stays the same.'
terms.etymology: From 'Il Gattopardo' (The Leopard) by Lampedusa
terms.usage: The Risorgimento is often criticized as an exercise in gattopardismo.

terms.definition: Total work of art; a synthesis of all art forms (music, drama, poetry, visual arts) into a unified aesthetic experience.
terms.etymology: Gesamt (total) + Kunst (art) + Werk (work)
terms.usage: Wagner conceived his operas as Gesamtkunstwerke that would transform society.

terms.definition: A cozy, convivial atmosphere; the warmth of being with good people in a pleasant environment. More active and social than hygge.
terms.etymology: From gezel (companion) + -ig + -heid (quality)

terms.definition: Obligation — specifically the social duty owed to others by virtue of relationship and gift. The tension between giri (social obligation) and ninjō (human feeling, personal emotion) is the structural conflict of Edo literature and Kabuki tragedy: the character who must do what is right by their social obligations even when every human feeling cries against it. The concept identifies the domain where social structure and personal desire most painfully conflict — Japan's version of the tragic.
terms.etymology: Gi (義: righteousness, duty) + ri (理: reason, principle). The characters point to duty grounded in reason rather than mere custom.

terms.definition: Forced coordination or synchronization; the Nazi process of bringing all aspects of German society into ideological conformity with the regime.
terms.etymology: Gleich (same, equal) + Schaltung (switching, circuit)
terms.usage: The Gleichschaltung systematically eliminated independent institutions, unions, and political parties.

terms.definition: German limited liability company — the dominant form of German private company. Requires minimum €25,000 share capital. The most common corporate form in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. Governed by the GmbHG (GmbH-Gesetz). Partners' liability limited to their capital contributions.
terms.etymology: Gesellschaft (company) + mit beschränkter (with limited) + Haftung (liability).

terms.definition: The durable, transposable dispositions through which social position is inscribed in the body. Bourdieu's central concept: the habitus is not a conscious strategy but a practical sense — a feel for the game — that generates appropriate actions without deliberate calculation. It is how class reproduces itself below the threshold of ideology: through posture, speech rhythm, taste, the way one holds a fork. The child of the bourgeoisie does not decide to be confident; confidence is inscribed as a disposition before reflection begins.
terms.etymology: Latin habitus (condition, state, from habere: to have, to hold). Aristotle's hexis in Latin translation. Bourdieu recovered it from scholastic philosophy.

quotes.text: The habitus is necessity internalised and converted into a disposition that generates meaningful practices.
quotes.source: Pierre Bourdieu, The Logic of Practice, 1980

terms.definition: Thisness. Duns Scotus's concept for the principle of individuation — what makes this thing this particular thing rather than another. Not its matter (which could be rearranged), not its form (which could be shared) but its sheer particularity, its here-and-now singularity. Hopkins used it as the theological foundation of his poetics: the 'inscape' of things, their individual distinctiveness that reflects God's creative abundance.
terms.etymology: From Latin haec (this, feminine) + -ceitas (abstract suffix). Coined by Scotus c. 1300.

terms.definition: A quality of coziness and comfortable conviviality that engenders a feeling of contentment or well-being. The art of creating warmth and intimacy in everyday moments.
terms.etymology: From Old Norse hugga (to comfort, console)

terms.definition: The collective melancholy of Istanbul. Orhan Pamuk's concept in Istanbul: Memories and the City — distinguished from individual sadness, from German Trauer, from Portuguese saudade. Hüzün is the shared mood of a city mourning its own imperial decline: the peeling plaster of wooden yalıs, the Bosphorus in winter mist, the consciousness of having once been the centre of the world. It is not depression but a form of pride — the melancholy of those who carry a great past in a diminished present.
terms.etymology: From Arabic ḥuzn (sadness). The Turkish word acquired its collective, civilisational dimension through Pamuk's theorisation.

terms.definition: Independent legal reasoning. The process by which a qualified jurist derives a ruling from first principles (Quran, Hadith, analogy, consensus) rather than following established precedent. The door of ijtihad was said to have 'closed' around the 10th century — a claim disputed ever since. Islamic modernism is largely the argument that the door must be reopened.
terms.etymology: From jahada (to strive). Jihad shares the root — both are forms of strenuous effort.

terms.definition: The reason for getting up in the morning. The convergence of what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for — the point where these four circles overlap is ikigai. The Western popularisation has somewhat flattened it: the Japanese concept is less a diagram of fulfilment than a recognition that purpose is always found in relation — to others, to one's community, to the world — not through pure self-expression.
terms.etymology: Iki (生き: life) + gai (甲斐: worth, result, benefit). The suffix -gai transforms a noun into that which gives it value.

terms.definition: American corporation designation — indicates a company incorporated under state law. C-Corps are taxed separately from shareholders; S-Corps pass through income. Delaware is the dominant state of incorporation for public companies due to its developed corporate law (DGCL).
terms.etymology: Incorporated — formally constituted as a legal corporation.

terms.definition: ICC rules defining buyer/seller responsibilities in international trade. Current version: Incoterms 2020. Key terms: EXW (Ex Works), FOB (Free on Board), CIF (Cost Insurance Freight), DDP (Delivered Duty Paid). Determines risk transfer point, who arranges transport/insurance, customs clearance responsibilities.
terms.etymology: International Commercial Terms — published by ICC since 1936.

terms.definition: Inner emigration. The practice of German writers and intellectuals who remained in Germany during the Nazi period but withdrew into private, coded, or historical subjects — neither actively collaborating nor actively resisting. Contested after 1945: was it complicity or survival? Thomas Mann attacked it from exile; Ernst Jünger embodied it from within.
terms.etymology: Coined to describe those who 'emigrated inward' rather than leaving the country.

terms.definition: The educated class with a conscience. The Russian term names not merely the educated but those who feel a moral obligation toward social transformation — the class that reads, debates, and believes it owes something to the people. Its defining tension: educated enough to see the problems, marginal enough to be unable to fix them. The word migrated westward as a general term but has never shed its Russian political charge.
terms.etymology: From Latin intelligentia (understanding). The Russian intelligentsia was theorised by Boborkykin in the 1860s.

terms.definition: The hailing that constitutes the subject. Althusser's concept in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses: ideology operates not by forcing beliefs but by calling individuals into subject-positions. When the policeman shouts "Hey, you!" and someone turns around, they have recognised themselves as the addressed subject and thereby become one. The individual becomes a subject by accepting the call — ideology is the unconscious structure through which we live our imaginary relationship to real conditions.
terms.etymology: French: to call out to, to question. Political sense: to call a minister to account before parliament.

quotes.text: All ideology hails or interpellates concrete individuals as concrete subjects.
quotes.source: Louis Althusser, Lenin and Philosophy, 1970

terms.definition: Now-time. Benjamin's concept in the Theses on the Philosophy of History: revolutionary time is not the homogeneous empty time of progress but a present moment charged with the entire past — a moment where now and the past flash together in a constellation. Jetztzeit is the moment the oppressed can seize: "every second of time was the strait gate through which the Messiah might enter." Against historicism's narrative of progress, Benjamin posits the revolutionary interruption of now.
terms.etymology: Jetzt (now) + Zeit (time). Benjamin opposes it to the homogeneous Zeit of historicism.

quotes.text: Jede Sekunde war die kleine Pforte, durch die der Messias treten konnte.
quotes.source: Walter Benjamin, Theses on the Philosophy of History, XVIII, 1940

terms.definition: Joy of living; exuberant enjoyment of life and its pleasures.
terms.etymology: Joie (joy) + de (of) + vivre (to live)
terms.usage: The Impressionists captured a certain joie de vivre in their depictions of leisure.

terms.definition: Enjoyment that exceeds and undermines pleasure. Lacan's technical term — distinguished from plaisir (pleasure, the release of tension): jouissance is the enjoyment that hurts, the compulsive repetition beyond the pleasure principle. It is what keeps the subject returning to what damages them. Translated inadequately as 'enjoyment' or left untranslated. Politically: Žižek argues that ideology operates not through ideas but through the jouissance attached to cultural practices — what we enjoy in our way of life.
terms.etymology: French verb jouir (to enjoy, to come) + -ance. The word spans enjoyment, orgasm, and legal possession (jouissance of property).

terms.definition: The exemplary person, the noble one. Originally 'son of a lord' — Confucius democratised it: the jūnzǐ is defined not by birth but by character, learning, and conduct. The concept is the Confucian answer to the question 'what should a human being be?': someone who has cultivated humaneness (rén), who acts from inner virtue rather than external compulsion, whose very presence raises the moral level of those around them. Not a saint but an ideal of educated, ethical adulthood.
terms.etymology: Jūn (lord, ruler) + zǐ (son, person). The combination originally meant 'ruler's son' and was reinterpreted by Confucius.

terms.definition: The restrainer — the force that holds back the end of the world. Paul's 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7: "you know what is restraining him now." Schmitt applied it to political theology: the Holy Roman Empire as the katechon, the force that prevented the unleashing of the Antichrist. The concept names the conservative function of any empire or institution: its legitimacy rests not on justice but on restraint — the prevention of something worse. Every status quo power claims to be a katechon.
terms.etymology: Greek: present participle of katechein (to hold back, to restrain). From kata (down, against) + echein (to have, to hold).

terms.definition: Self-emptying. Paul's concept in Philippians 2:7: Christ 'emptied himself' (heauton ekenōsen) — taking the form of a servant, setting aside divine power. The theological paradox: omnipotence expressed as radical weakness. The concept underlies the tradition of Christian mysticism (Meister Eckhart's Abgeschiedenheit, the Cloud of Unknowing) and resurfaces in Keats's negative capability, Simone Weil's decreation, and Levinas's ethics of substitution.
terms.etymology: Greek kenoun (to empty) + -osis (process suffix). From kenos (empty).

terms.definition: I am the state; attributed to Louis XIV, expressing the absolute identification of monarch and nation.
terms.etymology: L'État (the state) + c'est (is) + moi (me)
terms.usage: Whether or not Louis XIV said it, the phrase captures the essence of absolutism.

terms.definition: The Library of Babel. Borges's 1941 story: the universe is a library containing all possible books — every combination of letters that fits within 410 pages. Somewhere it contains the true catalogue of all catalogues, the perfect map of the library itself, the book that is the key to all books. Most books are meaningless. The librarians have spent their lives searching. The concept is the philosophical thought-experiment underlying every library, every archive, every search engine: the relationship between information and meaning, between the set of all possible statements and the subset that is true.
terms.etymology: Babel: the tower (Genesis 11), where language was scattered. The library contains all languages and all books — including the ones that explain the others.

terms.definition: Gap, hole, pit. In textual scholarship: a missing or illegible portion of a manuscript. Extended: any gap in knowledge, argument, or record. The lacuna is not simply absence but absence with a shape — you can see where something was. Scholarship is largely the study of lacunae.
terms.etymology: From lacus (lake, pit). The medical term for a small cavity derives from the same root.

terms.definition: Just the right amount; not too much, not too little. A Swedish philosophy of balance and moderation in all things.
terms.etymology: Possibly from Old Swedish lag (law, team) - 'according to the team'

terms.definition: The French doctrine of strict separation between religious institutions and the public sphere — more demanding than the Anglo-American concept of secularism. Not merely tolerance but the positive exclusion of religion from public life and state institutions. The 1905 law. The headscarf debates. A specifically French resolution of the Enlightenment's demand for universalism over particular identity.
terms.etymology: From laïc (layman, non-clerical), from Greek laos (people). The opposite is clérical.

terms.definition: Life-world; the pre-theoretical world of immediate experience, prior to scientific abstraction. The foundation of all knowledge and meaning.
terms.etymology: Leben (life) + Welt (world)
terms.usage: Husserl developed the concept of Lebenswelt to ground scientific knowledge in lived experience.
sources: Husserl - Die Krisis der europäischen Wissenschaften

terms.definition: American business structure combining corporate limited liability with partnership tax treatment. Flexible structure governed by state law. Members (not shareholders) own the company. Operating agreement defines governance. Delaware and Wyoming are popular formation states.
terms.etymology: Limited Liability + Company.

terms.definition: UK/US hybrid business form combining partnership flexibility with limited liability. Popular for professional services firms (law, accounting). Partners not personally liable for other partners' negligence. UK form governed by Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000.
terms.etymology: Limited Liability + Partnership.

terms.definition: Holding the world together. The Bhagavad Gita's concept of action done not for personal gain but for the maintenance of the cosmic and social order. Krishna tells Arjuna: even though I have nothing to gain, I continue to act — because if I did not, these worlds would fall apart. The concept founds a political ethics of duty without self-interest: the ruler governs not for power but to prevent disintegration. Weber's ethics of responsibility is its secular Western descendant.
terms.etymology: Loka (world) + saṃgraha (holding together, collecting). Appears in Bhagavad Gita 3.20–25.

terms.definition: UK private limited company — cannot offer shares to the public. No minimum capital. The standard form for UK businesses. Governed by Companies Act 2006. Requires at least one director and one shareholder.
terms.etymology: Limited — referring to limited liability of shareholders.

terms.definition: Ritual propriety, ceremony, the web of correct conduct. The Confucian claim that civilisation is not built on law or force but on the fine-grained network of proper behaviour: the right gesture at the right moment, the correct form of address, the appropriate ceremony for each occasion. Lǐ is not mere etiquette — it is the argument that form is prior to content, that the rituals that structure human interaction are not decoration but foundation. Confucius: if names are not correct, speech does not accord with truth.
terms.etymology: Oracle bone script: a vessel for ritual offerings. The meaning expanded from religious ceremony to all structured human conduct.

terms.definition: Sincerity, truthfulness — the Shinto ethical ideal. Not mere honesty but the complete alignment of inner state and outer expression, word and deed. Motoori Norinaga connected it to mono no aware: the sincere person is the one who can feel the pathos of things, who is not armoured against reality by convention or calculation. In Japanese aesthetics, sincerity is the ground from which genuine art grows — the poet who writes without makoto produces only technique.
terms.etymology: Made of the character for word (言) and becoming/completion (成): words that become true, speech that fulfils itself.

terms.definition: Bad faith; in Sartrean existentialism, the phenomenon of deceiving oneself about one's freedom and responsibility, pretending to be determined when one is free.
terms.etymology: Mauvaise (bad) + foi (faith)
terms.usage: Sartre illustrated mauvaise foi through the example of the waiter who plays at being a waiter.

terms.definition: Remember that you will die; a reminder of mortality meant to inspire humility and proper priorities.
terms.etymology: Memento (remember) + mori (to die)
terms.usage: Memento mori imagery proliferated in medieval and Baroque art.

terms.definition: Imitation, representation. The founding concept of Western aesthetics — art as the imitation of nature or action. Plato distrusted it: the painter imitates appearances which are themselves imitations of Forms. Aristotle rehabilitated it: through mimesis, tragedy achieves catharsis. The entire debate about whether art represents or creates reality turns on this word.
terms.etymology: From mimeisthai (to imitate). The mime, mimic, and mnemonic share the root.

terms.definition: The infinite mirror. Heraldic term for a shield bearing a smaller image of itself — extended by André Gide to literature: the work that contains a representation of itself within itself. Hamlet's play-within-a-play. Las Meninas. The footnote that comments on its own footnote. The device that makes the frame visible.
terms.etymology: From the heraldic expression for placing a figure 'in the abyss' of a shield — i.e., at its centre.

terms.definition: Co-guilt, shared guilt. The complicity of bystanders — those who did not perpetrate crimes but whose silence, indifference, or passive participation enabled them. Jaspers's moral guilt is the philosophical elaboration. Mitschuld is the guilt of the person who looked away, who did not ask, who accepted.
terms.etymology: Mit- (with, co-) + Schuld (guilt). The co- prefix is precise: not full guilt but shared implication.

terms.definition: Face — the socially granted kind. Distinguished from liǎn (moral character face, which is intrinsic): miànzi is reputation, prestige, social standing — granted by others and destroyable by them. To give face is to affirm someone's social worth publicly; to lose face is to be exposed as less than one claimed. The concept structures Chinese social and political interaction more completely than any written rule. It is not vanity — it is the recognition that the social self is constituted by the gaze of others.
terms.etymology: Miàn (face) + zi (nominalising suffix). Conceptualised by sociologist Hu Hsien Chin in 1944.

terms.definition: No-mind — the state of action without deliberate thought. The Zen ideal of the master swordsman, calligrapher, or archer: the practitioner who has internalised technique so completely that self-conscious deliberation drops away, and action flows without the interference of ego. Mushin is not mindlessness but a higher order of attentiveness — what Csikszentmihalyi calls flow, but in a Zen frame: the dissolution of the boundary between actor and action.
terms.etymology: Mu (無: nothing, non-) + shin (心: mind, heart). Also written mushin no shin — no-mind mind.

terms.definition: The world's capacity to make itself appear self-sufficient. Not simple illusion — māyā is the extraordinary power (śakti) by which Brahman produces the appearance of a world of separate, real things. The problem is not that the world doesn't exist but that we mistake its mode of existence: we take the relative for the absolute, the conditioned for the unconditioned. Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta: the world is neither real (as Naïve realism claims) nor unreal (as nihilism claims) but indescribable (anirvacanīya).
terms.etymology: Sanskrit root mā (to measure, to create). Related to Latin mirus (wonderful) and English 'magic.'

terms.definition: Deferred action, afterwardness. Freud's concept that trauma does not operate at the moment of occurrence but is constituted retroactively — a later event rewrites the earlier one, giving it its traumatic meaning. The past is not fixed; it is continuously revised by the present. Lacan emphasised it: the subject's history is not what happened but what is constructed from what happened. The concept dissolves the linear model of cause and effect in psychic life.
terms.etymology: Nach (after) + träglich (from tragen, to carry). The sense: that which is carried after, or which comes to bear afterward. Laplanche and Pontalis introduced it to English as 'afterwardness.'

terms.definition: Nobility obligates; the idea that privilege entails responsibility. Those born to wealth and power have a duty to act generously and honorably.
terms.etymology: From Old French, literally 'nobility obliges'
terms.usage: The concept of noblesse oblige underpinned aristocratic paternalism.

terms.definition: The originary act of land-seizure that founds all law. Schmitt's concept in The Nomos of the Earth: before there can be law there must be a taking (Nahme) — the violent appropriation of land that establishes the spatial order within which norms become possible. International law rests on the jus publicum Europaeum — the European states' agreement about how to divide the rest of the world. In classical Greek, nomos meant both law and pasture — the distribution that is also a habitation.
terms.etymology: Greek nomos (law, custom, pasture). Schmitt's concept of Ur-Nahme (originary seizure) is deliberately etymological.

terms.definition: The reclamation of African identity and cultural value against assimilation. Aimé Césaire and Léopold Sédar Senghor's concept (1930s): the refusal of the colonial demand to become French, the affirmation of African culture, aesthetics, and history as sources of value rather than deficits to be overcome. The concept's internal tension: Senghor's version risked essentialising African identity; Sartre called it a "negative moment" in the dialectic that would be superseded. Fanon criticised it as a bourgeois nationalism that left colonial structures intact.
terms.etymology: Négritude: from nègre (the reclaimed slur) + -itude (abstract suffix). The act of reclaiming the insult is constitutive of the concept.

quotes.text: Ma négritude n'est pas une pierre, sa surdité ruée contre la clameur du jour.
quotes.source: Aimé Césaire, Cahier d'un retour au pays natal, 1939

terms.definition: Coquettish withdrawal that demands pursuit. The beloved's power to withhold — knowing that withdrawal intensifies desire. In the ghazal tradition, nāz is not cruelty but a structural feature of love: the lover requires the obstacle. Extended politically: the sovereign's nāz is the refusal of easy access that produces reverence. The opposite is niyāz — the lover's need, the supplicant's submission. The two terms define the entire axis of Persian lyric.
terms.etymology: Persian. Cognate with Sanskrit nāṭya (performance). The concept has no Western equivalent.

terms.definition: Defamiliarisation — making the habitual strange. Shklovsky's concept in Art as Technique (1917): the purpose of art is to restore the sensation of life, to make us feel things rather than merely recognise them. Habit kills perception; art kills habit. Tolstoy describes a flogging as if seeing it for the first time, without the softening of familiarity. Brecht's Verfremdungseffekt is its theatrical version: the actor who reminds the audience they are watching a play, preventing the comfortable identification that produces passive consumption.
terms.etymology: From stranny (strange, odd) + the prefix o- (making something). Shklovsky coined it in the manifesto Iskusstvo kak priyom.

quotes.text: Цель искусства — дать ощущение вещи как видение, а не как узнавание.
quotes.source: Viktor Shklovsky, Art as Technique, 1917

terms.definition: Fearless speech. The obligation to speak truth to power, regardless of risk. Foucault's concept in his late lectures: the parrhesiastes (truth-teller) must be in a position of danger — speaking down to equals costs nothing. The Socratic obligation. The whistleblower's burden. A mode of speech that requires courage as its precondition.
terms.etymology: Pan- (all) + rhesis (speech). Complete speech — holding nothing back.

terms.definition: The Roman Peace; the period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius (27 BC - 180 AD).
terms.etymology: Pax (peace) + Romana (Roman)
terms.usage: The Pax Romana enabled commerce, cultural exchange, and the spread of Christianity.

terms.definition: Practical wisdom. Aristotle's intellectual virtue specific to action: the ability to deliberate well about what to do in particular circumstances, given the ends of a good human life. Not rule-following but judgment — the capacity to perceive what the situation requires. It cannot be taught by lecture; it is formed by practice and experience.
terms.etymology: From phronein (to think, to be minded). Related to phren (mind, diaphragm — the Greeks located thought in the chest).

terms.definition: Drug, remedy, and poison simultaneously. Plato's Phaedrus uses it for writing: Thoth offers writing to Pharaoh as a remedy for memory, but Pharaoh refuses — writing will weaken memory, not strengthen it, by offering an external substitute for internal recall. Derrida's reading: the pharmakon cannot be fixed as either remedy or poison because it is the condition of the distinction itself. Every technology of memory is also an instrument of forgetting.
terms.etymology: Greek: drug, medicine, poison, magical charm. The same word for cure and disease.

terms.definition: UK public company — shares may be offered to the public and traded on stock exchanges. Minimum £50,000 share capital. Governed by Companies Act 2006. Must have at least two directors. Suffix 'plc' required in company name.
terms.etymology: Public (shares available to public) + Limited (liability) + Company.

terms.definition: Fullness of power. The papal claim, developed by Innocent III and Innocent IV, that the pope holds absolute sovereign authority — spiritual and temporal — over the entire Christian world. The doctrine that produced the most extreme medieval claims to universal jurisdiction. Its theoretical limits were contested by canonists, bishops, and emperors for three centuries. The modern concept of sovereignty — absolute, indivisible, above law — is its secularised descendant.
terms.etymology: Plenitudo (fullness) + potestatis (genitive of potestas, power). First formulated by Pope Leo I (5th c.), systematised in the 13th.

terms.definition: The specifically Russian category of the vulgarly self-satisfied — kitsch that does not know it is kitsch, banality pleased with itself, the false and the sham presenting themselves as the real and the refined. Nabokov: "a special kind of smug, philistine vulgarity." Not mere bad taste but the complacent enjoyment of second-hand emotions and borrowed ideas, the aesthetic and ethical failure of a person who does not notice their own shallowness. Gogol is the great anatomist of poshlost'.
terms.etymology: Old Russian poshlyi: ordinary, common. The word degraded from "common" to "vulgar" to "smug-vulgar."

quotes.text: Poshlost is not only the obviously trashy but mainly the falsely important, the falsely beautiful, the falsely clever, the falsely attractive.
quotes.source: Vladimir Nabokov, Nikolai Gogol, 1944

terms.definition: Singapore private limited company — the dominant corporate form. Maximum 50 shareholders, shares not publicly traded. Minimum one director (Singapore resident), one shareholder, and company secretary. Governed by Companies Act. Registered with ACRA, assigned UEN (Unique Entity Number).
terms.etymology: Private Limited — Singapore adaptation of UK corporate terminology.

terms.definition: The place where one feels most oneself. From bullfighting: the spot in the ring where the bull returns for safety — from which it fights with most authority and confidence. Extended: the space, place, or activity from which a person draws their deepest sense of self. Not nostalgia but a present-tense orientation.
terms.etymology: From querer (to love, to want). The querencia is the loved place.

terms.definition: Whatever it pleases, anything whatsoever. The scholastic disputation in which the master was obliged to answer any question from any questioner — no topic could be refused. The institutional form that produced the most radical medieval philosophy, because the obligation to answer anything forced engagement with impossibly difficult problems. Agamben recovered the concept in The Coming Community: the 'whatever being' (essere qualunque) — the being that belongs to no category, that is not this or that but simply whatever — as the figure of a politics beyond identity.
terms.etymology: Latin quod (what) + libet (it pleases). The quodlibetal disputation was held twice yearly at major universities.

terms.definition: Reason of state; the principle that the state's interest justifies any action, including those that would otherwise be immoral.
terms.etymology: Raison (reason) + d'état (of state)
terms.usage: Richelieu elevated raison d'état above religious considerations in French policy.

terms.definition: The aesthetic theory of emotional essences. Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra identifies eight permanent emotional states (sthāyibhāvas) — love, humour, compassion, fury, heroism, terror, disgust, wonder — that art distils into pure aesthetic experience. The ninth rasa (śānta, tranquillity) was added by Abhinavagupta. Rasa is neither the emotion itself nor its representation but the generalised, purified essence that the connoisseur (rasika) experiences — a disinterested aesthetic enjoyment impossible in ordinary life. Abhinavagupta connects it to liberation (moksha).
terms.etymology: Sanskrit: juice, essence, taste. The metaphor is gustatory: aesthetic experience as flavour.

terms.definition: Politics based on practical and material factors rather than ideological or moral considerations; pragmatic power politics.
terms.etymology: Real (realistic) + Politik (politics)
terms.usage: Bismarck's Realpolitik unified Germany through calculated diplomacy and war.

terms.definition: A sense of hostility directed toward an object one identifies as the cause of one's frustration. In Nietzsche's philosophy, the resentment of the weak toward the strong, which inverts values.
terms.etymology: From Old French 'resentir' (to feel strongly)
terms.usage: Nietzsche traced the origins of slave morality to ressentiment against the masters.

terms.definition: Passive revolution — transformation without rupture. Gramsci's concept for political change managed from above to prevent change from below: the ruling class that incorporates enough of the revolutionary programme to defuse the revolutionary pressure. The Risorgimento was a passive revolution: national unification without the agrarian revolution that would have required the peasantry. Fascism was a passive revolution. Every managed reform that co-opts the radical demand while neutralising the radical movement is a rivoluzione passiva.
terms.etymology: Gramsci's term, derived from Cuoco's analysis of the failed Neapolitan revolution of 1799.

terms.definition: French public limited company — the form for large corporations and listed companies. Minimum €37,000 capital (€225,000 if publicly traded). Requires at least 7 shareholders. Two governance options: conseil d'administration or directoire with conseil de surveillance.
terms.etymology: Société anonyme — anonymous company, meaning shareholders are not personally liable.

terms.definition: French limited liability company — equivalent to GmbH or LLC. Partners' liability limited to contributions. Flexible structure for small and medium enterprises. Requires at least one associate (associé), no minimum capital since 2003.
terms.etymology: Société (company) + à responsabilité limitée (with limited liability).

terms.definition: French simplified joint-stock company — highly flexible corporate form popular for startups and subsidiaries. No minimum capital, great contractual freedom in organizing governance. The dominant form for venture-backed French companies.
terms.etymology: Société par actions (joint-stock company) + simplifiée (simplified).

terms.definition: Enlightenment — the sudden, irreversible recognition of one's original nature. The specifically Zen kind: not gradual progress toward a goal but an abrupt breakthrough (kenshō) that cannot be prepared for by accumulation. The koan is the instrument: an impossible question (what is the sound of one hand clapping?) that frustrates discursive reason until the mind breaks through to a different mode of knowing. Satori cannot be described to those who have not experienced it — and descriptions of it are obstacles to those who have not.
terms.etymology: Japanese: from satoru (to understand, to be enlightened). The character 悟 combines mind/heart (心) with the phonetic component.

terms.definition: Longing for what is absent and may not return. Neither nostalgia (which knows its object) nor ennui (which lacks an object) but the specific ache of the absent that was loved — a person, a country, a time, a possibility. The word is contested as uniquely Portuguese: it appears in Galician-Portuguese lyric poetry of the 13th century. Fado is its musical form. Manuel de Melo (1635): 'um bem que se padece.'
terms.etymology: Disputed: possibly from Latin solitudo (solitude) or salvus (safe, whole). The Galician-Portuguese troubadours used soidade.

terms.definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
terms.etymology: Schaden (damage, harm) + Freude (joy)
terms.usage: Nietzsche analyzed Schadenfreude as a manifestation of ressentiment.

terms.definition: Thus, so. The parenthetical that says: I know this looks wrong, but I am quoting accurately — the error belongs to the original. [sic] is the scholar's most precise gesture of distancing. It does not correct; it marks the boundary between the editor's responsibility and the text's. Every [sic] contains a judgment.
terms.etymology: Latin adverb sic (so, thus). Often written in brackets: [sic].

terms.definition: The copy without an original. Baudrillard's concept: in hyperreality, representations no longer refer to a reality they represent — they constitute their own reality. The map precedes the territory. Disneyland exists to make the rest of America seem real. The Gulf War did not take place — not because it didn't happen but because the media event and the military event had become indistinguishable.
terms.etymology: From Latin simulacrum (likeness, image). Plato's cave is the original problem; Baudrillard is its postmodern solution.

terms.definition: Communal unity. The Slavophile concept of a specifically Russian form of collective life — organic, spiritual, consensual, rooted in the Orthodox Church community (sobor = council, cathedral). Against Western individualism and rationalism. The concept was recovered by Soviet ideology (in secularised form) and by 20th-century Russian nationalism. The permanent Russian alternative to liberal individualism.
terms.etymology: From sobor (assembly, council, cathedral). The Slavophiles developed it in the 1840s.

terms.definition: Event — the philosophical category that erupts into and transforms the given situation. The Russian word contains within it the structure of Badiou's concept: so-bytie (co-being, being-together). Bakhtin's concept of the event of being: ethical life cannot be reduced to abstract norms; it is always the unrepeatable event of this encounter, this moment of responsibility. The event is what forces a decision — what divides time into before and after.
terms.etymology: Russian: event, occurrence. Literally so-bytie: co-being. The prefix so- (together, co-) adds the communal dimension.

terms.definition: Solitude that aches. Not simply aloneness — soledad is inhabited, productive, sorrowful. The solitude of the flamenco singer, the desert mystic, the exile. Machado (Antonio): 'caminante, son tus huellas el camino y nada más.' The concept is embedded in Spanish Romanticism and the Generation of '98's diagnosis of Spain's historical isolation.
terms.etymology: From Latin solitudo (solitude). The suffix -edad intensifies into a condition, not merely a state.

terms.definition: Studied carelessness; the art of performing difficult tasks with such ease that they appear effortless. A Renaissance ideal of aristocratic grace.
terms.etymology: From Italian 'sprezzare' (to disdain)
terms.usage: Castiglione advocated sprezzatura as essential to the perfect courtier.

terms.definition: The redirection of sexual and aggressive drives toward culturally valued ends. Freud's concept: civilisation is built on the sublimation of drives — art, science, and philosophy are forms of redirected libidinal energy. Leonardo's painting is sublimated sexuality. The concept is simultaneously flattering (art is powerful) and deflating (art is substitute). Lacan refined it: sublimation raises an object to the dignity of the Thing — it does not redirect the drive but transforms its aim.
terms.etymology: From Latin sublimare (to elevate, to lift up). Chemical term: solid directly to vapour without liquid phase — Freud used the analogy deliberately.

terms.definition: The highest good; the ultimate end or purpose of human life, variously identified as happiness, virtue, pleasure, or God.
terms.etymology: Summum (highest) + bonum (good)
terms.usage: Every ethical system must define its conception of the summum bonum.

terms.definition: Blank slate; the theory that the mind at birth is empty of innate ideas, all knowledge coming from experience.
terms.etymology: Tabula (tablet) + rasa (scraped, blank)
terms.usage: Locke's tabula rasa doctrine challenged rationalist theories of innate knowledge.
sources: John Locke - Essay Concerning Human Understanding

terms.definition: The Reorganisation. The Ottoman reform programme of 1839–1876 — a sustained attempt to modernise the empire's legal, administrative, and educational structures along European lines while preserving Ottoman sovereignty. The Gülhane Edict (1839) guaranteed rights to all subjects regardless of religion. The project's structural failure: reforms advanced enough to delegitimise the old order but not enough to replace it. Every late colonial modernisation is a Tanzimat.
terms.etymology: Arabic tanzīm (organisation, ordering) in Ottoman Turkish. The period is also called the Era of Tanzimat.

terms.definition: The limit before which / after which. Scholarly tools for dating: the terminus post quem is the earliest possible date (the thing cannot be earlier than X); the terminus ante quem is the latest possible date (it cannot be later than Y). Between the two termini lies the possible. All historical knowledge is framed by termini.
terms.etymology: Terminus (boundary, end point) + ante (before) / post (after) + quem (accusative of qui, which).

terms.definition: The taste of a place. Originally wine: the specific combination of soil, climate, slope, and microclimate that makes a Burgundy untranslatable. Extended to cheese, bread, language, character — the claim that place is not background but ingredient. Against globalisation's axiom that the particular can always be reproduced elsewhere.
terms.etymology: From terre (earth, land). First used in viticulture; generalised in the 20th century.

terms.definition: Contemplation, beholding. The activity of pure intellectual vision — disinterested inquiry into what is, for its own sake. Aristotle's highest life. The Greek word was also used for the official delegations sent to consult oracles and attend festivals — the word for metaphysical contemplation and civic embassy is the same. Theory and public life were not yet separated.
terms.etymology: From theōros (spectator) + -ia. Theōros is from thea (sight, view) + horan (to see).

terms.definition: The official delegation sent from a city to consult an oracle, witness a festival, or observe foreign customs — the same word as theoretical contemplation. The theōros was simultaneously a spectator and an ambassador: seeing on behalf of others, reporting back what was witnessed. This doubles the etymology of theory: knowing by seeing, seeing on behalf of a community. Nightingale's Spectacles of Truth argues that the philosophical concept of theōria was constructed against this civic practice of spectating.
terms.etymology: Theōros (spectator, official delegate) + -ia. From thea (sight) + horan (to see). Also the root of theatre (theatron: place for seeing).

terms.definition: Repair of the world. Kabbalistic concept: the material world is broken — sparks of the divine light are scattered, trapped in shells (kelipot). Human action — ethical, ritual, mystical — gathers and restores the sparks. In modern liberal Judaism, secularised as the obligation to social justice. The two meanings (mystical cosmology and political ethics) are both active simultaneously.
terms.etymology: Tikkun (repair, correction) + olam (world, eternity). The phrase appears in the Aleinu prayer.

terms.definition: The Mandate of Heaven. The Zhou dynasty doctrine justifying the overthrow of the Shang: the divine order confers legitimacy on rulers who govern virtuously and withdraws it from those who do not. Natural disasters, social unrest, and military defeat are signs that the mandate has been lost — not causes of the loss but symptoms of it. The concept makes legitimacy radically conditional: there is no divine right that cannot be forfeited. Every Chinese dynasty collapse has been retrospectively explained as mandate-withdrawal.
terms.etymology: Tiān (heaven, sky, the natural-divine order) + mìng (fate, command, mandate). Developed by the Duke of Zhou (c. 1042 BCE).

terms.definition: Gate-closing panic. The anxiety that time is running out — that a gate is closing and you will be left outside. Used especially for the fear of missed life milestones: marriage, children, career achievement. The medievally-literal German encodes an entire psychology of foreclosure.
terms.etymology: Tor (gate) + Schluss (closing) + Panik (panic). The closing gate of a walled city before nightfall.

terms.definition: Anguished longing with nowhere to go. Nabokov: 'No single word in English renders all the shades of toska. At its deepest and most painful, it is a sensation of great spiritual anguish, often without any specific cause. At less morbid levels it is a dull ache of the soul, a longing with nothing to long for.' Toska is Weltschmerz without the idealism — pure ache.
terms.etymology: Old Slavic. Related to tesnota (tightness, constriction) — the sensation of being pressed.

terms.definition: Comrade — the word that tried to replace all others. The Bolshevik address that abolished "mister," "master," and all titles of rank: everyone is a comrade. The concept carries the entire project of revolutionary equality in a single word of address.
